newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada seen keeping inflation low for years.
newsitem.headline: Canada seen keeping inflation low for years.

text.p: Canada is likely to maintain one of the lowest inflation rates in the industrialised world for several years, with its currency and bonds benefiting as a result, analysts said on Tuesday.
"I'm bullish on inflation over the next few years here, and certainly relative to the U.S.," said Dan Kelly, a financial market analyst with CIBC Wood Gundy Securities. "Inflation is dead in Canada."
A government report released on Tuesday confirmed that inflation pressures remain subdued.
Statistics Canada reported that consumer prices excluding food and energy, the so-called core CPI, rose just 1.3 percent in October year over year.

The report shows that inflation in Canada remains near the bottom of the Bank of Canada's target range of 1 percent to 3 percent and is the second lowest in the Group of Seven industrial nations after Japan.
Canada's inflation rate is now less than half that of the United States and the rate has been lower than U.S. inflation since 1992.

"I think, looking forward, the prospects for sustained low inflation are very, very good," said Michael Gregory, an economist and strategist with Lehman Brothers in Toronto. "The implications for financial markets, I think, are positive."

The main factor expected to keep inflation subdued is the Bank of Canada's long-stated commitment to price stability. The central bank has fought since the late 1980s to reduce inflation and the 1-percent-to-3-percent target band for inflation will remain in place until the end of 1998.

Some economists have recently suggested that the central bank raise that target band slightly in order to "lubricate" the economy and increase job creation. But Bank of Canada Governor Gordon Thiessen firmly opposes that view. Earlier this month, Thiessen made it clear he had no plans to alter the bank's tough stand on inflation.
The current target range comes up for review next year and will be discussed at a policy conference to be held by the bank in the spring.

A rise in the target band for the inflation rate can be all but ruled out, financial market analysts said. Instead, the debate at the bank has shifted to whether the current targets should be maintained or lowered even further.

"There's no way that the Bank of Canada is going to step aside from its price stability policy. It's hard-won credibility," said Harvinder Kalirai, Canadian analysts with New York-based financial analysis firm I.D.E.A.
That credibility suggests inflation will average no more than 2 percent from now until the end of 1998, and Canadians will gradually begin to see the benefits of that, analysts said.
Canada's dollar can be expected to slowly appreciate in value because of low inflation during the next three years, said CIBC Wood Gundy's Kelly.
Long-term borrowing costs for Canadians should also decline relative to other countries as Canada extends its low inflation record, said Carl Weinberg, chief economist with High Frequency Economics.

"We are thinking now of Canada as pricing itself based on its own domestic fundamentals and not at a markup over the U.S.," said Weinberg. "With 1 percent inflation there's no reason why short-term interest rates couldn't be at 2 percent and bond yields couldn't be at 3 or 4 percent. And that's something that all Canadians can benefit from."
